transcript.content: Hi, I'm Dr. Smith. Welcome in—what brings you here today?

Hello, Dr. Smith. Thank you, um, thank you for seeing me. I suppose the short answer as to what brings me in is my sleep, or rather, the absolute lack of it. It’s become completely unmoored. And when I say unmoored, I mean it has entirely lost its anchor to any normal human schedule. 

It’s been a bit of a progression, you see. At first—and this was quite a departure for me—I was waking up after only two, maybe three hours of sleep. But the peculiar thing was, I didn't feel tired in the slightest. I would wake up in the pitch black, and my mind would just be... illuminated. I’d get right out of bed, go straight to my study, and I’d be up drafting all these elaborate plans, feeling absolutely ready to go. I felt like I had the stamina of a man thirty years younger, just this boundless drive to get things done while the rest of the world was asleep.

But then... well, it shifted. It shifted on me. Now, I’m still waking up long before dawn, but that vitality is completely gone. I just lie there in the dark, staring at the ceiling, and my stomach is just... it's tight, tied up in these awful knots. I'll lie there for hours, listening to the house settle, just waiting for the sun to come up, and I have absolutely no sense of rest whatsoever. None at all. It’s just this agonizing, hollow exhaustion, and I simply can't seem to turn it around, no matter what I try.
During that earlier time when you were staying up all night full of energy, did you also notice your mood becoming unusually elevated, euphoric, or irritable—more than just having extra energy?

Well, "elevated" is... it’s almost too small a word for it, Dr. Smith. It was a profound, almost—well, a brilliantly optimistic state of mind. For weeks on end, I walked around with this absolute, unshakeable certainty about everything I was doing. You know how normally in life, especially at my age, you weigh the hurdles before you embark on a project? Well, during that period, every single obstacle, every logistical problem that might normally give a man pause, it all just seemed utterly trivial. I’d look at a complex issue and think, 'Child's play, easily managed,' and just brush it aside. 

But—and I suppose this gets to the heart of what you're asking—it wasn't all just pleasant euphoria. Not at all. Because if anyone, and I mean absolutely anyone, dared to question my methods or my ideas... well, my patience was entirely nonexistent. I didn't just disagree with them, I snapped at them. Quite viciously, I'm ashamed to admit now. It felt entirely justified in the moment, of course. I felt as though they were being willfully obtuse, as if they were actively trying to sabotage the only sensible man in the room. I just couldn't fathom how they couldn't see the sheer, obvious brilliance of what I was putting together, so I'd lash out at the slightest hint of hesitation or critique on their part. It was this very strange dichotomy, you see, being so completely on top of the world, so expansive in my thinking, yet so fiercely, fiercely intolerant of anyone who wasn't on my exact wavelength.

During this current period of feeling hollow and exhausted, have you experienced anything like hearing voices, seeing things that others don't, or having beliefs that others tell you aren't true—such as feeling convinced you've done something terribly wrong or that something bad is going to happen to you?

No, no, nothing like hearing voices or seeing things. My mind isn't playing tricks on me in that way, Dr. Smith. It’s... it's much more grounded in reality, unfortunately. But the beliefs... well, you ask about feeling convinced I've done something terribly wrong. And the truth is, I *have*. I have done something terribly, irrevocably wrong. 

It’s this investment decision I made during that... that period of boundless confidence we were just discussing. I keep replaying it, over and over and over again in my mind, especially during those long, dark hours before dawn when I can't sleep. Every detail of it, every conversation with the broker, every document I signed. I just lie there and tell myself, with absolute certainty, that I have completely ruined my wife’s security. We had a plan, you see. A very careful, conservative plan for our retirement, built over decades of hard work and prudent saving. I was always the responsible one. Always. Friends, family, they all looked to me as the steady hand, the one who never took foolish risks. 

And then... I just threw it all away on this grand scheme that I was so profoundly convinced was foolproof. I made a fool of myself, but worse, I made a fool of a lifetime of being the responsible one. I’ve compromised everything we built. It’s not a delusion, Doctor, it’s a fact. The guilt of it is just... it’s suffocating. It sits on my chest like a physical weight. I look at my wife, and she doesn't know the full extent of it yet, and I just feel this overwhelming, crushing sense of worthlessness. How could a man of my age, with my education, be so incredibly reckless? I should have known better. I did know better, for sixty-eight years of my life. And now... now I’ve just ruined it all. It’s all I can think about. It just circles and circles in my head until I feel like I'm losing my mind, but not because I'm hearing voices, just because the reality of what I've done is so unbearable.
Given how overwhelming this guilt and worthlessness feels, have you had any thoughts of harming yourself or that you would be better off dead?

Well, Dr. Smith... that is... that is the crux of it, isn't it? The sheer weight of it all. You ask about thoughts of... of not being here. And I have to be honest, as difficult as it is to admit aloud. Yes. Yes, I have. 

It’s not so much a dramatic, active plan, if you understand my meaning. It’s more of a... a pervasive, creeping darkness. There are mornings, particularly after those endless nights of staring at the ceiling and cataloging every single mistake I’ve made, when the first light starts to filter through the blinds, and the thought just settles over me like a heavy blanket. I think... I think it would just be such a profound relief if I simply did not wake up. If the burden of facing my wife, of facing the reality of our diminished future, was just... lifted. 

I’ve never been a man to run from his responsibilities. As I said, sixty-eight years of being the steady hand. But the shame of this... it’s so consuming that the idea of just slipping away quietly seems almost like a kindness. A kindness to myself, and perhaps, in a twisted sort of logic, a kindness to her, so she wouldn't have to look at the man who squandered her security. 

It got to a point a few days ago—and this is what truly terrified me, Doctor—where the thoughts weren't just a passive wish anymore. They were becoming louder, more insistent. I was standing in the garage, looking at some old rope from my sailing days, and I realized... I realized I was actually contemplating the mechanics of it. That frightened me. It frightened me so deeply because it was so antithetical to everything I am, or at least, everything I thought I was. It scared me enough that I went inside, sat my wife down at the kitchen table, and I told her. I couldn't bring myself to tell her about the money yet, the full extent of the ruin, but I told her about the darkness. I told her, quite plainly, that I did not trust myself. I said, 'Margaret, I should not be left alone right now.' And bless her, she hasn't left my side since. But the thoughts... they are still there, hovering at the edges, waiting for a moment of weakness.

When your wife or others point out that the investment loss, while serious, hasn't actually left you destitute or ruined your entire retirement, are you able to consider that perspective at all, or does it feel absolutely certain and unshakeable no matter what anyone says?

Well, Dr. Smith... Margaret... bless her heart, she tries. She really does try to tell me exactly that. She’ll sit there at the kitchen table, holding my hand, and she’ll say things like, "We still have the house, we have my pension, we aren't going to be out on the street," and so on. She tries to be the voice of reason. But... it just doesn't penetrate. It's like she's speaking a foreign language to me. 

Because, as I was trying to explain a moment ago, the reassurances just don't change the fundamental reality of what I did. I just keep replaying that investment decision. Over and over. Every single morning, every afternoon, every night. I sit in my armchair and I trace it all back to that one specific phone call, that one signature on the wire transfer. And no matter what financial documents she tries to show me to prove we aren't entirely destitute, I am just telling myself, with absolute, unshakeable certainty, that I have ruined my wife’s security. 

You see, it's not merely about the exact dollar amount left in the checking account, though God knows the loss is substantial enough. It's the profound failure of it all. For my entire life, through my years in graduate school, through my entire career before I retired... I was the man people came to for sound, rational advice. I was the rock. The careful one. And to have thrown all that away... to have made an absolute fool of a lifetime of being the responsible one... how do you possibly put a positive spin on that? You simply can't. 

So when you ask if I can consider their perspective... no. I really can't. They can talk until they're blue in the face about how we will survive this, but it doesn't erase the fact that I squandered the safety net I promised her. It's like a film reel stuck on a loop in my brain, just playing that moment I made the decision, and the guilt is just... it's absolute. It doesn't matter what anyone says to comfort me, because the truth of my own foolishness is the only thing that makes sense anymore.

Because, as I was trying to explain a moment ago, the reassurances just don't change the fundamental reality of what I did. I just keep replaying that investment decision. Over and over. Every single morning, every afternoon, every night. I sit in my armchair and I trace it all back to that one specific phone call, that one signature on the wire transfer. And no matter what financial documents she tries to show me to prove we aren't entirely destitute, I am just telling myself, with absolute, unshakeable certainty, that I have ruined my wife’s security. 

You see, it's not merely about the exact dollar amount left in the checking account, though God knows the loss is substantial enough. It's the profound failure of it all. For my entire life, through my years in graduate school, through my entire career before I retired... I was the man people came to for sound, rational advice. I was the rock. The careful one. And to have thrown all that away... to have made an absolute fool of a lifetime of being the responsible one... how do you possibly put a positive spin on that? You simply can't. 

So when you ask if I can consider their perspective... no. I really can't. They can talk until they're blue in the face about how we will survive this, but it doesn't erase the fact that I squandered the safety net I promised her. It's like a film reel stuck on a loop in my brain, just playing that moment I made the decision, and the guilt is just... it's absolute. It doesn't matter what anyone says to comfort me, because the truth of my own foolishness is the only thing that makes sense anymore.

inference.note: The patient's unshakeable, fixed conviction that he has 'ruined' his wife's security—maintained with absolute certainty despite factual reassurance and evidence to the contrary—meets criteria for a mood-congruent delusion (of guilt/poverty) rather than simple depressive rumination. Combined with the prior hypomanic/manic episode with grandiosity and irritability, this supports a current major depressive episode with psychotic features within bipolar disorder, ruling out F31.4 (severe without psychotic features).
